title: Catch-up: everything so far in plain words
summary: Thirty days with the maths taken out. Text becomes arrows, documents get cut into pages, a graph walk finds the nearest page without reading all of them, and quantisation shrinks the numbers. Plus an honest list of what you can forget from the last two weeks.
html:
Thirty lessons in. The last fifteen of them went hard into index internals, and if a lot of that went past you, that is on me rather than on you. So today there is nothing new. This is the whole course so far with the maths taken out, and an honest list of what you can forget.

Read it in fifteen minutes. If a section here makes sense, the harder lesson behind it has already done its job and you do not need to go back to it.

What changes from today

Three things, because you were right to push on this.

Lessons get shorter and plainer. Fifteen to twenty minutes, one idea each, and the idea comes first in ordinary words before any notation. The measurements stay, because numbers I ran myself are the reason this course is worth more than a blog post, but from now on they live in a block at the end that you can skip without losing the lesson.

Marking a day done now means writing a note. Four lines in a file on GitHub. Until today the tick box lived in your browser's local storage, which means it was invisible to me, so I had no idea whether you were reading any of this. The note fixes that in both directions: I can see it, and it tells me what landed.

The note is a commit, so it shows on your contribution graph. You asked for proof of consistency on your profile. Two minutes of typing a day, committed from your own account, is real proof. Me pushing lessons to the repo is not the same thing and I will not pretend otherwise.

One: text becomes arrows

A computer cannot compare the words "dog" and "puppy". It can compare numbers. So every piece of text gets turned into a list of numbers, and that list is an arrow pointing somewhere in space.

Take the smallest possible example. Two words in the whole language, "dog" and "cat". Three documents:

                   dog   cat
A  "dog dog"         2     0
B  "cat cat"         0     2
C  "dog cat"         1     1

A points along one axis, B along the other, C sits between them at 45 degrees. Similarity is the angle: A and C are 45 degrees apart, A and B are 90 degrees apart, so A is closer to C than to B. That is cosine similarity, and that is all it is. The 1 and the 2 do not matter much, which is why we normalise the arrows to the same length and compare direction only.

Real embeddings do the same thing with 384 or 768 numbers instead of two, and the numbers come out of a trained model instead of word counts. The model's trick is that it puts "dog" and "puppy" at a small angle even though they share no letters. Everything in days 3 through 14 is that one trick, plus how the model is trained to get it.

Two: the book gets cut into pages

You do not retrieve documents, you retrieve pieces of them. A forty page policy document has one paragraph that answers the question, and handing the model all forty pages buries it.

So you cut. A thousand word document into two hundred word chunks gives you five pieces. Make them overlap by forty words and you get six, because the overlap costs you a bit of duplication and buys you insurance: the sentence that answers the question is no longer sitting exactly on a cut line with half its context on the other side.

That is the entire chunking trade. Smaller chunks mean sharper matching and less context. Larger chunks mean more context and blurrier matching, because one arrow now has to represent five different topics and ends up pointing between all of them.

Three: finding the nearest page without reading all of them

Say you have a million chunks, each a 768 number arrow. Four bytes a number, so about 3 KB per arrow and roughly 3 GB in total. The honest way to answer a query is to compare it against all million. That means reading 3 GB of memory for every single question. It works, it is exactly correct, and it is too slow once you have traffic.

The way out is a shortcut that is usually right. Build a graph: every chunk gets linked to its sixteen nearest neighbours. To search, start anywhere, look at your current node's neighbours, step to whichever one is closest to the query, and repeat until no neighbour is closer. You end up in the right neighbourhood having looked at maybe a thousand nodes out of a million.

The analogy that actually fits: you are in a city looking for one specific person, and everyone knows their sixteen closest friends. You ask whoever is nearest, they point you to the friend who lives closest to your target, and you walk. A few hops and you are on the right street. Nobody had a list of everybody.

That is HNSW. The layers, the ef parameter and the pruning rules from days 17 to 20 are tuning on top of this one idea. If the paragraph above makes sense, you have the useful part.

Four: making the numbers smaller

3 GB of arrows is awkward and expensive to keep in memory. Quantisation is the family of tricks for storing an approximate arrow in far fewer bytes.

The crudest version makes the point. Keep only the sign of each number: positive becomes 1, negative becomes 0. Your 768 numbers at 4 bytes each, 3,072 bytes, become 768 bits, which is 96 bytes. Thirty two times smaller. Comparing two of them is counting how many bits differ, which a CPU does in a couple of instructions.

You have thrown away a lot and the ranking gets noticeably worse. So you use it as a first pass: let the cheap version pick 100 candidates out of a million, then score those 100 properly with the full arrows. The expensive step now runs 100 times instead of a million. Product quantisation from days 22 to 25 is a cleverer version of the same two step bargain.

What you can forget

Genuinely forget, and look it up on the day you need it:

  • The bandwidth arithmetic from day 15. It answers "why is brute force slow", and you now have that answer in words.
  • The rotation in OPQ on day 25. It is a refinement worth a few percent.
  • The percolation threshold from day 30. The rule of thumb is the part that matters: filtered graph search breaks when the filter is very selective, so switch strategies there.
  • The residual trick in IVF-PQ on day 24, and the confidence interval procedure. Both are methodology you can pick up again when you are running your own experiments.

Three things worth keeping instead:

  • Recall, latency and memory are one budget. Every index decision spends from it. Nothing is free and anyone claiming otherwise is selling something.
  • You cannot tell whether a change helped without a baseline and a measurement. Most of this course is really about that habit.
  • Approximate search can return the wrong neighbour. For search that is usually fine, and knowing it is fine is what lets you take the speedup.

Five questions

Answer them in your head, then read the next line. If you get three, you are in good shape.

  1. Why normalise an embedding before comparing? So length stops mattering and only direction counts.
  2. What does chunk overlap buy? Insurance against the answer landing on a cut line.
  3. Why is brute force search slow at a million vectors? Every query has to read every vector, gigabytes of memory per question.
  4. What does a graph index actually avoid doing? Looking at most of your data.
  5. Why would you ever search with a worse representation of your vectors? To cheaply shortlist candidates, then score the shortlist properly.
If you remember one thing
Everything in the last thirty days was one question: how do you find the right page without reading the book. Counting words, cutting chunks, walking graphs and shrinking numbers are four answers to it.

Tomorrow we are back to new material, and it gets more practical from here. Phase 3 is techniques you can put in a system next week rather than index internals.
